newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha defiant as Albania parties work on crisis.
newsitem.headline: Berisha defiant as Albania parties work on crisis.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha signalled a tough stance on Sunday in efforts to end a deadlock over planned elections, opposing changes to election laws that have forced most parties to threaten to boycott the vote.
As Berisha spoke to rallies of supporters of his Democratic Party in the north, politicians in the capital kept up efforts to find a compromise over the elections.

The June 29 election is the key element in a drive to restore order to Albania, engulfed by riots and lawlessness earlier this year after thousands of people lost life savings in the collapse of crooked pyramid investment schemes.
Berisha told his supporters that he did not agree with demands to amend the election law, which most political parties say favour Berisha and the Democrats and want changed.
"I will not decree their requests," he told the rally in the town of Lac, 45 km (30 miles) north of Tirana.
Prime Minister Bashkim Fino meanwhile had asked for written opinions from parties on proposed changes to the law, made in an ultimatum to Berisha late on Saturday by the parties.
"We are expecting views from each party, which will be considered by the government and all the other parties who suggested the changes," Fino's spokesman said.

Most parties of Fino's Government of National Reconciliation, formed in March to calm the rioting, want the election law to be changed to take control of the election away from Berisha and put in the hands of the government.

The parties' ultimatum to Berisha included a list of demands including the nomination of the electoral commission by the government, changes in voting districts and a legal definition of the status of international monitors.
They also wanted the head of the Shik secret police and the head of the radio and television council, which controls electronic media, to be named within three days.
The parties want to make sure that the secret police are neutral in the elections and also prevent the single nationwide television station exclusively championing the Democrats.
The debate continued under strong pressure from Western governments, which say that if compromise is not found for free and fair elections then international aid may be cut off.
There have been calls from the European Union, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and Italy, which leads a multinational U.N.-mandated force protecting aid supplies.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Sunday he had told Albania's parties that the whole future of their country was at stake in the pre-election crisis.

"In these days, in the last few hours, I have continued to have contact with all the Albanian parties and the different forces represented in Albania to highlight to them the importance of an accord to hold the elections on time," he told reporters in the northern town of Modena.
Italy has several times warned that the multinational force, seen as a stabilising factor in the volatile country, may be withdrawn if the elections do not go ahead.

The international community wants to avoid a repeat of May 1996 elections, which international observers said were deeply flawed. The Socialists boycotted the vote on its last day, leaving Berisha's Democratic Party the dominant force in parliament.
In the latest spasm of anarchic violence afflicting Albania, an armed gang battled with police reinforced by armoured cars in the southern town of Tepelene on Sunday, local residents said.
Three passers-by were caught up in the battle and received gunshot wounds, they added.
They said that a gang of at least 15 men swept into Tepelene, 200 km (120 miles) from the capital Tirana, shooting wildly at the police station and demanding that police hand over their weapons.
But the police fought back and drove the gang into another town nearby where they were being contained.
